newsitem.title: ITALY: INA plans to lower Banco Napoli stake - MD.
newsitem.headline: INA plans to lower Banco Napoli stake - MD.

text.p: INA plans to eventually lower its holding in Banco di Napoli once the southern Italian bank has been fully privatised, the chairman of the Italian insurer said in an article published in Corriere della Sera newspaper.
The Treasury announced at the weekend that it had sold a 60 percent stake in Banco di Napoli to INA and Banca Nazionale del Lavoro for 61.6 billion lire.
INA's stake in the joint partnership is 51 percent while BNL has a 49 percent holding, however BNL is expected to eventually fuse with Banco di Napoli.
"I do not believe that it is INA's role to maintain a controlling position in the new banking group once the privatisation objective has been reached," INA's Sergio Siglienti wrote in the newspaper.
"I believe INA will have an active role until (privatisation) has been achieved, after which it should dilute its holding," he added.
The government has said it wants to sell its remaining 40 percent holding in troubled Banco di Napoli as soon as possible.

The sale of the majority stake in the southern bank to recently privatised INA and Treasury-controlled BNL has been dubbed by many commentators a "false" sell-off, with Banco di Napoli staying firmly in state hands.
However Siglienti said there had been no alternative.
"Right now Banco di Napoli, principally for reasons of profitability, cannot be sold on the market and even less so, in one block to foreign investors," he said.
The Treasury received just two bids when it offered Banco di Napoli at auction -- one offer from INA/BNL, the other from state owned credit institute Mediocredito Centrale.
Despite the situation at Banco di Napoli, which has lost some six trillion lire over the past three years, Siglienti said it was important for his company to take a holding in the group.

"Our institute was alone among major Italian insurance companies not to have a bank-based distribution network," he said. He added that the sale terms had been: "undoubtedly favourable". --Rome newsroom +396 678 2501
